artists.biography:
Suede are an English alternative rock band from London, formed in 1989. The group's most prominent early line-up featured singer Brett Anderson, guitarist Bernard Butler, bass player Mat Osman and drummer Simon Gilbert. By 1992, Suede were hailed as "The Best New Band in Britain", and attracted much attention from the British music press. The following year their glam rock-inspired debut album, Suede, went to the top of the charts, became the fastest-selling debut album in almost ten years and won the Mercury Music Prize, helping kick-start the Britpop movement. However, the band's lush follow-up, Dog Man Star (1994), saw Suede distance themselves from their Britpop peers. Although it is often regarded as the band's masterpiece, the recording sessions for Dog Man Star were fraught with difficulty, and ended with Butler departing the band after heated arguments with Anderson.
In 1996 following the recruitment of Richard Oakes and later keyboardist Neil Codling, Suede went on to greater commercial success with Coming Up. The album charted at number one in the UK, producing five top ten singles and became their biggest-selling album worldwide. In 1997, Anderson became addicted to crack and heroin. Despite problems within the band, Suede's fourth album Head Music (1999) was a British chart-topper. Suede's final album, A New Morning (2002), their first after the collapse of Nude Records, was a commercial disappointment, and the group disbanded the following year. After much speculation Suede reformed in 2010 for a series of concerts.

perplexity.description:
Suede's self-titled debut album, released in March 1993 on Nude Records, stands as a landmark record in British rock history. The album synthesizes glam rock aesthetics with alternative rock sensibilities, drawing comparisons to David Bowie and The Smiths through its combination of shimmering, melodic guitar work and introspective, often provocative lyrics. Guitarist Bernard Butler's compositions provide the musical foundation—characterized by tinkling piano interludes, pounding rhythms, and primal guitar parts—while singer Brett Anderson's lyrics explore themes of sex and depression with an urgency that reflected the band's youthful intensity.

The album's commercial and critical success was immediate and substantial. It became the fastest-selling debut album in British history in nearly a decade, debuting at the top of the UK Albums Chart and winning the 1993 Mercury Music Prize. The three lead singles—"The Drowners," "Metal Mickey," and "Animal Nitrate"—generated significant media momentum before the album's release, establishing Suede as central figures in the emerging Britpop movement. Opening with "So Young," a glam rock-inflected track that balances hedonistic confidence with vulnerability, the album showcases Butler and Anderson's complementary creative partnership, with Butler handling the majority of melodic composition while Anderson contributed the lyrical content.

Despite its immediate impact, the album's trajectory was complicated by territorial disputes; its US release faced legal injunctions at the time. Nevertheless, Suede established the band's artistic identity and commercial viability, positioning them as one of the first and most critically respected acts of the Britpop era, a status that would be reinforced by their subsequent albums throughout the 1990s.
